claims.text: The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy has good room-temperature performance but inadequate high-temperature strength.
Adding approximately 1–2 at% Ti will promote nucleation of Ti-rich precipitates.
The precipitates produced by Ti microalloying will be fine, nanoscale, and coherent.
Fine precipitates contribute to grain refinement by retarding grain-boundary motion.
Fine precipitates block dislocation motion and thereby provide precipitation strengthening.
Fine precipitates stabilize grain boundaries against coarsening through a pinning or drag effect.
Dislocation pinning, grain refinement, and grain-boundary stabilization will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
The Ti-induced precipitates will improve creep resistance.
The precipitates will resist coarsening sufficiently during elevated-temperature exposure to avoid a loss of room-temperature ductility.
A 1–2 at% Ti addition will retain room-temperature ductility similar to that of the baseline.
The limited Ti addition will keep the alloy density low and cause only a minimal density increase relative to the baseline.
Ti microalloying will increase high-temperature yield strength by approximately 15–20% relative to the unmodified alloy.
The proposed strengthening and creep benefits should hold at 900–1100°C under tensile and creep loading.
The beneficial effects occur only within a narrow Ti range of approximately 1–2 at%.
Higher Ti concentrations may cause excessive precipitate formation or precipitate coarsening.
Higher Ti concentrations may deteriorate room-temperature ductility.
Higher Ti concentrations may increase density beyond acceptable limits.

contradictions.description: The predicted yield-strength gain is 15–20%, but the falsification threshold is below 10%; a result between 10% and 15% would miss the stated prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
